PullRequest.Title: workbench: auto-hide sash grippers when the mouse is idle
PullRequest.Body: ## Summary - Make sash grippers quiet at rest in the editor's Modern UI and the Agents window, revealing them when the mouse moves. - Add `workbench.sash.autoHideGrippers` (default `true`) and `workbench.sash.autoHideGrippersDelay` (default `2000` milliseconds). Both apply immediately without reloading. - Fade out over 300 ms and fade in over 150 ms, respecting reduced motion. Resize hit targets and existing hover/drag feedback remain unchanged. - Track activity independently for each window, including auxiliary windows and ordinary webview content. No linked issue was provided; this implements a maintainer-requested UI improvement. ## Issues addressed | Severity | Issue | Resolution | |---|---|---| | P2 | Movement inside ordinary webviews did not reach the owning window's idle tracker. | Forward trusted, position-changing activity through the existing webview bridge, coalesced once per animation frame. | | P2 | Redispatching queued webview movement as mouse input could move an active sash unexpectedly. | Use a dedicated activity-only notification, with regression coverage for queued delivery during a real sash gesture with auto-hide on and off. | | P2 | Motion selectors missed workbenches where the motion and Modern UI classes share the same root. | Match both root arrangements and test intermediate opacity, asymmetric fade durations, and reduced motion. | ## Validation Validated on macOS arm64, Node.js 24.22.0, Code OSS 1.144.0 Dev. | Command | Result | |---|---| | `npm run build-fast -- --client-only` | Passed. | | `npm run typecheck-client` | Passed. | | `npm run eslint -- src/vs/sessions/test/browser/sessionGridLayout.test.ts src/vs/workbench/contrib/sash/browser/sash.ts src/vs/workbench/contrib/sash/browser/sash.contribution.ts src/vs/workbench/contrib/sash/test/browser/sash.test.ts src/vs/workbench/contrib/webview/common/webview.ts src/vs/workbench/contrib/webview/browser/webviewElement.ts src/vs/workbench/contrib/webview/test/browser/webviewElement.test.ts src/vs/workbench/contrib/webview/test/node/webviewShellMessaging.test.ts` | Passed without warnings. | | `npm run stylelint -- src/vs/workbench/browser/media/style.css src/vs/workbench/contrib/modernUI/browser/media/sashHandles.css src/vs/sessions/browser/media/workbench.css` | Passed; eight advisory suggestions concern existing declarations in the shared stylesheet. | | `npm run valid-layers-check` | Passed. | | `git diff --check` | Passed. | Focused regression command: ```sh ./scripts/test.sh \ --run src/vs/base/test/browser/ui/sash/sash.test.ts \ --run src/vs/workbench/contrib/webview/test/browser/webviewElement.test.ts \ --run src/vs/workbench/contrib/webview/test/node/webviewShellMessaging.test.ts \ --run src/vs/workbench/contrib/sash/test/browser/sash.test.ts \ --run src/vs/sessions/test/browser/sessionGridLayout.test.ts \ --run src/vs/workbench/contrib/modernUI/test/browser/modernUI.contribution.test.ts \ --grep 'WebviewElement|Webview shell messaging|Sash|Sessions - Grid Layout|sash|grip' \ --reporter dot ``` Result: **104 tests passed**. Covers exact idle thresholds, custom/zero delays, live setting changes, disposal, window isolation, queued webview activity during resizing, gripper styling in both workbenches, and reduced motion. ### How to test 1. Enable the editor's Modern UI, or open the Agents window. 2. Move the mouse: grippers should fade in. Stop moving: after two seconds, they should fade out. 3. Resize a pane before and after the dots hide; the resize target and hover/drag highlight should be unchanged. 4. Set `workbench.sash.autoHideGrippersDelay` to another value and verify the new delay without reloading. 5. Disable `workbench.sash.autoHideGrippers` to retain the existing persistent gripper appearance. 6. Verify ordinary Markdown Preview movement resets the timer and activity in one window does not affect another. 7. Enable reduced motion and verify opacity changes are immediate. ## Visual evidence ### Editor grippers after the same idle period Comparable images were captured from the actual merge-base revision `b2a378625354d01407b9673aa63e911d8d729a37` in a separate detached worktree and from this reviewed branch. Both use Dark 2026, the same README workspace and window dimensions, the same pointer position, and 2800 ms without movement. ## Review status - Final local review: no unresolved actionable findings in the approved scope. - Accepted limitation: movement inside nested frames embedded in webviews, including cross-origin Simple Browser pages, is not detected. This is documented in the setting description. The experimental hover fallback was removed at the maintainer's direction rather than shipping an unreliable exception. - Validation limits: native auxiliary-window interaction, Windows/Linux, and the full smoke/integration suites were not exercised. Auxiliary-window lifetime and isolation have focused regression coverage. - Required remote CI and manual image attachments are not yet verified.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The complete message path from capture listener through rAF, MessagePort, WebviewElement handler, and CustomEvent is explicit. The absence of a consumer when auto-hide is disabled and the limited CSS consumers are also directly established; only the exact platform-dependent cost per message is uncertain.
Findings.PerformanceResource: cross-frame MessagePort posts, structured-cloned payload objects, host message dispatch, and CustomEvent objects
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Continuous movement over one webview produces one boundary message per animation frame (typically 60-120 per second) for the duration of movement, regardless of whether auto-hide is disabled or the owning workbench renders these grippers.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: avoidable cross-context message traffic and main-thread CPU/GC pressure during webview interaction
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before this PR, webview mouse movement did not send a did-mouse-move message through the webview MessageChannel and did not allocate and dispatch a host-window CustomEvent.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The preload now always captures mousemove and posts did-mouse-move once per animation frame. WebviewElement always consumes each post and dispatches a CustomEvent, while SashGrippersController has no activity listener when workbench.sash.autoHideGrippers is false; the CSS consumers are additionally limited to modern-ui and agent-sessions-workbench roots.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: Added line 767 introduces the frame-coalesced MessagePort post for mouse movement; added listeners at lines 957 and 1233 make this path unconditional for shell and content movement.
Findings.Title: Gate the webview mouse bridge before sending frame-rate messages
Findings.Impact: Moving the pointer over common webviews such as Markdown preview generates frame-rate MessagePort and host event work even after the user disables auto-hide, and also in workbench states with no applicable gripper styling. This wastes renderer/main-thread capacity and battery on an interaction path where the messages cannot affect UI.
Findings.Evidence: The added rAF callback posts did-mouse-move at lines 760-770 through HostMessaging's MessageChannel/MessagePort implementation (lines 307 and 329). WebviewElement handles every message and constructs/dispatches a CustomEvent at lines 248-250. By contrast, SashGrippersController returns before installing its webview activity listener when the setting is false (sash.ts lines 96-98). Repository search shows --sash-grip-opacity is consumed only by modernUI sashHandles.css and sessions workbench.css, so other roots also cannot use the traffic.
Findings.Recommendation: Make activity forwarding subscription-based: have the host enable it only while the owning container has applicable gripper UI and auto-hide enabled, and disable it immediately with the setting/UI state. When enabled, send an immediate reveal plus bounded heartbeat/trailing activity sufficient to maintain the idle deadline instead of one boundary post every animation frame.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The listener-to-timer call path and default-enabled registration are explicit in the diff, and browser pointer events commonly arrive many times per frame. Exact CPU cost varies by platform, which affects severity, but the repeated timer/allocation mechanism and its hot-path reachability are certain.
Findings.PerformanceResource: browser timeout registrations/cancellations and per-event position objects on the window mousemove path
Findings.PerformanceScaling: The work runs once for every distinct mousemove sample in each active window; high-polling mice can produce hundreds to roughly a thousand samples per second during ordinary pointer movement.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: continuous CPU and GC pressure on a latency-sensitive input path, with avoidable timer-queue churn while the pointer is moving
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before this PR there was no global sash-gripper mousemove tracker, no idle timeout to recreate, and no per-sample position object allocation.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The new capture listener sends every changed pointer position to showGrippers; showGrippers clears the current timeout, removes the class, and creates a fresh timeout for every sample, even though after the first sample the grippers are already visible and only the eventual idle deadline changes.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: Added lines 103-110 introduce unconditional clearTimeout and setTimeout calls inside showGrippers, and added lines 116-123 invoke that function from every distinct global mousemove sample.
Findings.Title: Keep one idle deadline instead of rebuilding the timer per mouse sample
Findings.Impact: With the default-enabled setting, normal pointer movement anywhere in the workbench repeatedly cancels and allocates timers at hardware event frequency. This can consume main-thread time and generate garbage during input even though visible state changes only on the first movement and after the user becomes idle.
Findings.Evidence: registerContainer installs a window-level capture mousemove listener at line 123. Each changed coordinate allocates lastMousePosition and calls showGrippers (lines 116-121), which unconditionally clearTimeout/classList.remove/setTimeout (lines 103-110). ILayoutService documents one container per window, so this is one hot listener per workbench window rather than per sash; the realistic multiplicity is pointer sample rate. The CSS state itself changes only when entering/leaving idle, making the intervening timeout rebuilds redundant.
Findings.Recommendation: Record the latest activity timestamp, reveal only on the visible-state transition, and keep a single timeout whose callback either hides or reschedules for the remaining deadline. This preserves hiding autoHideDelay after the final movement without canceling/recreating a timer or allocating a position object for every sample.

Scenarios.Scenario: Ordinary pointer movement in a workbench or auxiliary window while sash gripper auto-hide is enabled
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The capture-phase window mousemove handler runs synchronously during each pointer event; it deduplicates identical coordinates, then clears and recreates the idle timer before event dispatch completes. The eventual hide callback is asynchronous.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Distinct pointer samples while moving. Effective cardinality is one handler invocation and one timeout cancellation/registration per changed coordinate per active workbench window, commonly hundreds of samples per second and potentially around 1000 Hz with high-polling devices.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Events are processed serially on each window's main thread. Each window owns an independent tracker; repeated events replace one pending timeout rather than accumulating concurrent callbacks, but replacement work is unbounded by a throttle.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: There is no cache. Exact duplicate screen coordinates are suppressed, but every real coordinate change repeats the full timer operation; cold and sustained movement behave the same after the first reveal.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the new global listener directly invokes unconditional clearTimeout/setTimeout and allocates a new position object for every distinct sample.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Timer and allocation cost varies by browser, pointer hardware, and movement duration; the global hot-path multiplicity is established, so uncertainty affects severity rather than mechanism confidence.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable repeated-work regression because the PR adds timer-queue and allocation churn at raw input frequency although visible state changes only at idle/activity transitions.

Scenarios.Scenario: Pointer movement inside an ordinary WebviewElement such as Markdown Preview
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The webview capture listener schedules an animation-frame callback; that callback must post through the transferred MessagePort, the host must dispatch its handler and CustomEvent, and the sash controller must process activity before hidden grippers are revealed. The first step is deferred to the next frame, but all downstream work consumes renderer/host main-thread time during interaction.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Post did-mouse-move through the webview shell's transferred MessagePort, structured-clone the coordinates, process the host handler, and dispatch a host-window CustomEvent.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One call per animation frame during real pointer movement after within-frame coalescing, typically 60-120 per second for one hovered webview.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The scenario sent no mouse-activity MessagePort messages and dispatched no corresponding host CustomEvents before the diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The message is required for gripper reveal when the feature is active, but when auto-hide is disabled or no styled grippers apply it cannot advance user-visible work and is pure background overhead.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Duration of continuous movement times display refresh rate after rAF coalescing. Effective cardinality is one cross-frame post per active webview per animation frame, typically 60-120 posts per second; only the webview under the pointer normally generates activity.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: At most one rAF callback is pending per webview, so raw mouse samples are coalesced within a frame. There is no lower-frequency throttle or backpressure across frames; MessagePort events are processed serially by the host.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The last exact screen position is retained to suppress duplicates, and pending movement is coalesced within one frame. There is no subscription/configuration cache: forwarding remains active when auto-hide is disabled or no applicable styled grippers exist.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the preload listener, rAF coalescing, MessagePort implementation, host handler, and disabled-controller path were all traced directly.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Per-message cost depends on Electron/browser process placement and refresh rate, but the cross-context boundary, frame-rate cardinality, and no-consumer configurations are explicit.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable because the diff adds frame-rate boundary traffic unconditionally, including configurations where the feature has no consumer.

Scenarios.Scenario: Initial idle hide, configuration changes, auxiliary-window creation, and window disposal
Scenarios.CriticalPath: After the workbench is restored, each existing container installs listeners and starts one idle timeout; newly added containers do the same. Configuration changes synchronously clear/rebuild listeners and restart one timer. Window/container disposal synchronously clears the timer, listeners, and hidden class.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of open workbench windows/containers and infrequent setting changes. Effective cardinality is one controller store and one pending idle timeout per window.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Windows track independently with one timeout each. Configuration updates are serialized by the configuration event; no task burst or shared limiter is needed at realistic window counts.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cache is involved. Current configuration is read when each tracker is rebuilt, and disposal removes per-container state.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: layout service defines one container per window, and disposal ownership is explicit through container disposables plus onDidUnregisterWindow.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Users can open multiple auxiliary windows, but realistic counts are small and registration occurs after restored rather than on the startup critical path.
Scenarios.Verdict: No additional finding: startup/lifecycle work is O(windows), occurs after restoration, and cleanup cancels timers and removes listeners without retention.

Scenarios.Scenario: Idle-to-active CSS fade for Modern UI and Agents-window sash grippers
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The idle timeout toggles one root class; CSS custom properties update opacity/transition duration on applicable sash pseudo-elements. The first movement after idle removes the class and starts the fade-in; subsequent class removals while already active do not change DOM state.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of applicable top-level sash grippers in one workbench container and frequency of actual idle/activity transitions, not raw movement count for style mutations.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: CSS transitions for applicable grippers run together on the owning window; reduced-motion roots eliminate transition duration. There is no asynchronous boundary or explicit fan-out loop in JavaScript.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Browser style state is reused normally; no application cache exists. Hidden/visible state is represented by one root class, so one transition serves all grippers in the container.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: CSS consumers are limited to Modern UI and Agents-window selectors, and opacity is the only transitioned property.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The number of top-level sashes varies by layout but is small; browser style/compositor behavior varies by platform.
Scenarios.Verdict: No separate finding: one root class transition per idle/activity state change is bounded and aligned with the requested visual behavior; the reportable overhead is the repeated event/timer and webview messaging work between transitions.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 14 changed files and all diff pages. Traced global mouse input, per-window lifecycle, CSS state changes, and the webview MessagePort boundary. Submitted two diff-caused findings: raw-event idle-timer churn and unconditional frame-rate webview activity messages. No concrete cleanup leak, startup regression, unbounded retention, or additional rendering/layout regression was found.
